strategy.method: Improper-integral limit with an inverse-trig antiderivative
strategy.why_this_method: The integrand becomes unbounded at the upper endpoint, so the definite integral must be defined by a limit.
strategy.alternatives: A sine substitution also works, but it still requires an endpoint limit.

steps.title: Identify the improper endpoint
steps.explanation: The denominator vanishes at the upper endpoint. The integral cannot be evaluated by direct endpoint substitution.
steps.common_mistake: An integrable endpoint singularity still requires limit notation.

steps.title: Rewrite the integral as a limit
steps.explanation: Stop short of the singular endpoint at b. Then let b approach 1 from inside the interval.
steps.common_mistake: The approach must be from the left because the interval lies below 1.

steps.title: Use the inverse-sine antiderivative
steps.explanation: The integrand matches the derivative of inverse sine. Evaluate at the temporary endpoint before taking its limit.

steps.title: Evaluate the endpoint limit
steps.explanation: Inverse sine is continuous up to 1. The finite limit shows that this improper integral converges.
steps.common_mistake: A definite integral never receives a plus C.

final_answer.plain: The improper integral converges to pi over 2.
final_answer.domain_notes: The integrand is unbounded at x = 1, but the improper integral converges.

check.detail: The transformed bounds are 0 and pi/2 and the transformed integrand is 1.

hints: Inspect the denominator at both endpoints before integrating.
Replace the upper endpoint with b and take a left-hand limit.
The antiderivative before taking the limit is arcsin(b) - arcsin(0).
